newsitem.title: USA: U.S. steps up attack on Turkish premier.
newsitem.headline: U.S. steps up attack on Turkish premier.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday stepped up its attack on Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, accusing him of "taking pot shots" at America with "objectionable remarks" during a visit to Libya.
"It is rather unusual to speak this way about a NATO ally. But, frankly, given the circumstances ... we had no alternative," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.

Turkish media quoted Erbakan as saying on Sunday that Libya was "against terrorist activities" and was "the country suffering most from terror". He was speaking after being shown around a house belonging to Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi in Tripoli that had been hit during air strikes by U.S. warplanes in 1986.
Burns said on Monday the remarks were surprising if true, in what U.S. officials said was a "stiff rebuke" to Turkey's Islamist premier.

"I don't believe that the Turkish government has confirmed for the United States government these remarks," Burns said Tuesday. "But I can tell you, having looked at this fairly closely and having seen the consistent reporting from the Turkish press, that we stand by our remarks yesterday."
"We strenuously disagree with remarks from Prime Minister Erbakan which try to diminish the role and the responsibility that Muammar Gaddafi has for international terrorism," he said.

"We ought to try to ... promote an end to terrorism in Libya, rather than taking pot shots at the United States. So, these were objectionable remarks. They were heard in Washington. And, believe me, they are not welcome in Washington."
The United States and its allies hold Libya responsible for the bombing of Pan Am flight 103 over Scotland in 1988, which killed 270 people. Libya denies involvement.
Erbakan's Libyan visit caused an uproar in Turkey after Gaddafi called for an independent Kurdish state -- anathema to Ankara. Opposition politicians have demanded he resign.

The almost unprecedented public rebuke to Erbakan reflects intense U.S. anger over his flirting with Libya -- regarded in Washington as a rogue state -- and sense of betrayal after U.S. support for Turkey's bloody war against Kurdish separatists.
Burns said Washington would now seek a "private dialogue" with the Turkish government to seek out Ankara's position on issues such as terrorism, democracy and NATO cohesion.

"These are important issues that I think the Turkish prime minister needs to be reminded of," he said. "We're talking about Turkey coming back to an agreement with the United States that we ought to isolate Gaddafi."
